What ten years of tide records say about the bay

Volunteers have read the gauge in the port twice a day since 2016. The sea is four centimetres higher, and winter storms now reach the old town's walls.

AR

By Ana Ruiz

12 October 2026 6 min read

Contents

  1. How the readings were taken
  2. Four centimetres in ten years
  3. Storms that reach the walls
  4. What the council plans next

Since March 2016, a group of volunteers has read the tide gauge in the port at six in the morning and six in the evening, every day of the year. Their sheets, now ten years of them, are the longest record of the sea in the bay that anyone has kept by hand.

How the readings were taken

Each reading is the height of the water against the gauge, to the nearest centimetre, with the time, the wind and the state of the sea. Two people read it, and a third checks the sheet the same week. A reading that two people do not agree on is left out.

  • 7,300 readings a year, two a day.
  • 41 volunteers over ten years, nine of them from the start.
  • Fewer than one reading in a hundred left out.

The gauge itself is a post marked in centimetres, fixed to the quay in 1931. The port checks it against a survey mark every spring.

Four centimetres in ten years

The average height at high tide was 4 cm higher in 2025 than in 2016. That is close to the rise that the national tide gauges record along the whole coast, which gives the volunteers' figures some weight.

We did not set out to measure the climate. We wanted to know when to take the boats out.

Year to year the change is too small to see on the gauge: the waves move the water more than the sea rises. Only the average of thousands of readings shows it.

Storms that reach the walls

In the first five winters, waves reached the sea wall of the old town twice. In the last five, they reached it eleven times. Four of those were on spring tides with a south-west wind, the same pattern each time.

A few centimetres of sea matter most on those days: a wave that used to break on the beach now breaks on the wall.

What the council plans next

The council will publish the full records as open data in January and has asked the volunteers to add a third daily reading at noon. It will also put an automatic gauge beside the old one, so the two can be compared for a year.

Anyone can join the readings. The group meets at the harbour office on the first Monday of each month.
